items.title: Income tax cut to 4.99% with a path to 3.99% (Georgia Economic Growth and Tax Relief Act of 2026)
items.status: Signed by Gov. Kemp May 11, 2026; the 4.99% rate applies to tax year 2026
items.summary: Lowers Georgia's flat personal and corporate income tax rate from 5.19% to 4.99% for 2026, then by 0.125 percentage points a year toward 3.99% if state revenue benchmarks are met (about eight more years). Raises the standard deduction to $15,000 (single) and $30,000 (joint) for 2026, rising later to $18,000/$36,000; raises the dependent exemption from $4,000 to $5,000 (reaching $6,000 over time) and the retirement income exclusion from $65,000 to $70,000 beginning in 2027; and exempts up to $1,750 each in cash tips and overtime pay for 2026 through 2028. It also eliminates several income tax credits and sales and use tax exemptions (including one for pollution-control equipment) as of Jan. 1, 2026. Final passage April 2, 2026: House 104-71, Senate 33-20.
items.why: Opponents said the cut would 'blow a $6.5 billion hole in the state budget over time,' and Sen. Josh McLaurin (D-Sandy Springs) called it fiscally irresponsible (AJC). Gov. Kemp cited a revenue reduction of nearly $1 billion for FY2027 when he withheld more than $300 million in new spending. Further rate cuts depend on revenue benchmarks that the incoming governor and 2027 legislature will inherit.
items.sponsors: Rep. Shaw Blackmon (R-Bonaire), House Ways and Means chair

items.title: Property tax relief: mandatory homestead assessment cap and a new 1% Local Homestead Option Sales Tax (LHOST)
items.status: Signed by Gov. Kemp May 11, 2026; the mandatory assessment cap applies statewide starting with the 2027 tax year; no local LHOST acts were enacted in the June 2026 special session
items.summary: The 'Homeownership Opportunity and Market Equalization Act of 2026' makes the statewide homestead assessment cap (which limits annual increases in a home's taxable value to the inflation rate) mandatory by repealing local opt-outs, so it applies statewide as of the 2027 tax year. It lets counties, by local referendum, adopt a 1% Local Homestead Option Sales Tax (LHOST) whose proceeds fund a new homestead exemption, with any excess reducing millage rates, and it changes how existing FLOST revenue is applied. Proposed caps on local budgets were removed before final passage, and the Senate rejected the House's HB 1116 (a cap on growth in school and local levies of 3% or inflation, whichever is higher). In the June 2026 special session nearly 100 local LHOST acts were introduced, but none received the required two-thirds vote, so no LHOST acts were enacted.
items.why: The assessment cap reaches every jurisdiction starting in 2027, but the LHOST sales-tax swap cannot begin until local acts pass, so those acts would have to come back in the 2027 session. A companion bill, SB 566, requires tax bills and assessment notices to show the savings from exemptions and creates a statewide homestead exemption database at the Department of Revenue.
items.sponsors: Carried in the House by Rep. Shaw Blackmon (R-Bonaire); Senate sponsor not confirmed in sources opened

items.title: FY2027 state budget ($38.5 billion) with a $300 million-plus spending freeze
items.status: Signed by Gov. Kemp May 12, 2026; fiscal year began July 1, 2026
items.summary: The General Assembly passed a $38.5 billion state budget for the year beginning July 1, 2026 (House 153-5; Senate unanimous). It includes more than $70 million to put a literacy coach in every K-3 elementary school, almost $15 billion for K-12 basic education, $100 million for state employee retirement funding, $4 million for student mental health services, funding for 500 NOW/COMP disability waiver slots, 124 new medical residency slots, and a cut of about $34 million to the University System Board of Regents' proposed budget 'to reflect increased credit hour productivity for online courses.' On signing, Gov. Kemp directed agencies to withhold more than $300 million in proposed new spending, citing a revenue reduction of nearly $1 billion for the coming fiscal year from tax cuts. FOX 5 described the signed plan as a $36.6 billion budget, the figure the governor's release gives as the general fund revenue estimate.
items.why: This was Kemp's final budget as governor (FOX 5). WRDW reported the spending freeze scales back expansions including school bus operations, pre-K growth, doctor residency slots and waiver slots for Georgians with developmental disabilities. The FY2028 budget will be written under a new governor, with the income tax rate still scheduled to fall under HB 463.
items.sponsors: House Appropriations Chair Matt Hatchett; Senate Appropriations Chair Blake Tillery (budget leaders named by the Georgia Recorder)

items.title: Tax code conformity and a 60-day suspension of the state motor fuel tax
items.status: Signed by Gov. Kemp March 20, 2026; its 60-day fuel tax suspension ended May 19, and a May 15 executive order suspended the tax again May 20-June 3 (ratified by HR 3EX)
items.summary: Updates Georgia's income tax code to the federal Internal Revenue Code as of Jan. 1, 2026, while decoupling from several federal changes (the federal auto-loan interest deduction and the federal tips and overtime exclusions, among others). It also suspended the state motor fuel excise tax, which the Governor's office put at 33.3 cents per gallon of gasoline and 37.3 cents for diesel, for 60 days starting with the governor's signature. That suspension ended at 11:59 p.m. May 19; on May 15 Gov. Kemp declared a state of emergency and suspended the gas tax for two more weeks, May 20 through June 3. The Governor's office reported May net tax revenue fell 12.6% ($339.1 million), with motor fuel tax collections down $196.6 million.
items.why: Speaker Jon Burns estimated the 60-day suspension would save Georgians nearly $400 million (Governor's office); the legislature's June special session ratified the follow-up executive order (see HR 3EX).
items.sponsors: Rep. John Carson; carried in the Senate by Sen. Chuck Hufstetler

items.title: Keeps current voting machines through 2027, orders a new hand-marked ballot system plan, mandates close-race hand recounts
items.status: Final passage June 23, 2026 (House 94-79; Senate agreed 36-16); now law: members of the committee it created were announced July 28, 2026, and its report is due Jan. 31, 2027
items.summary: Passed in the June 2026 special session after the regular session failed to act, SB 3EX moves the deadline for ending QR-code ballot tabulation (set by a 2024 law for July 1, 2026) to Jan. 1, 2028, so the current touchscreen system stayed in place for the Nov. 3, 2026 election. It creates the Election Equipment Specifications and Standards Committee to recommend a new voting system to lawmakers during the 2027 session, including the use of hand-marked paper ballots produced by ballot-on-demand printing; its report is due Jan. 31, 2027. It also requires a statewide hand recount, reimbursed by the state if finished within 17 days, when a race for one of eight state constitutional offices (Governor, Lieutenant Governor, Secretary of State, Attorney General, School Superintendent, and the Insurance, Agriculture and Labor Commissioners) appears first or second on the ballot and is decided by 0.5% or less; on the Nov. 3, 2026 ballot that covers only the Governor's race. Federal races are not covered. It also widens risk-limiting audits to every federal race and the top statewide races (O.C.G.A. §§ 21-2-495(d.1), 21-2-498). A Senate Democratic amendment to force Democratic representation on the committee failed.
items.why: Without it, the 2024 ban on QR-code vote counting would have taken effect July 1, 2026 with no approved alternative counting method (AJC). Lawmakers are to receive the committee's voting-system recommendations during the 2027 session.
items.sponsors: Sen. Max Burns (R-Sylvania)

items.status: Included in Gov. Kemp's special session proclamation; legislative leaders declined to redraw maps and the session adjourned June 23, 2026; on Nov. 4, 2026 Kemp said he will not call a special session to redraw districts

Callais, along with election-system continuity, local homestead legislation and ratification of the fuel tax suspension. House and Senate leaders said before the session that they would not pursue new maps, and none were changed. The AJC reported Republican leaders feared a redraw would hand Democrats a campaign issue in November. On Nov. 4, 2026, Atlanta News First reported Kemp will not call a special session to redraw the state's political districts; Republican lawmakers had called for one after the U.S. Supreme Court narrowed the scope of the Voting Rights Act in April.
items.why: Current maps remain in place for now; Kemp said Georgia must adopt new maps before the 2028 election cycle, which leaves redistricting to the 2027 legislature and the incoming governor.
items.sponsors: Gov. Brian Kemp (proclamation)

items.title: Lets pharmacists prescribe birth control pills and shots
items.status: Signed by Gov. Kemp; the Georgia House announced May 14, 2026 that the bill became law (signing date not stated)
items.summary: The 'Increasing Access to Contraceptives Act' lets pharmacists at Georgia-licensed pharmacies and hospitals dispense self-administered contraceptives or administer injectable contraceptives without a doctor's prescription. GPB reported it covers pills and injections for patients 18 and older (younger patients must show a previous prescription). Sponsor Rep. Beth Camp cited 82 Georgia counties without an OB-GYN. A provision requiring folic acid fortification of corn masa was stripped before final passage. A separate bill allowing Georgians to get HIV-prevention medicine at their local pharmacy also passed on the session's final day.
items.why: Expands access to contraception statewide, including in the counties without an OB-GYN that the sponsor cited; GPB reported pharmacy availability would not begin until 2027, after the Department of Public Health and the State Board of Pharmacy agree on rules.
items.sponsors: Rep. Beth Camp (R-Concord); Senate sponsor Sen. Kay Kirkpatrick (R-Marietta)

items.status: Hearing held Sept. 1, 2026 on Georgia Power's direct testimony; the PSC calendar lists a hearing Nov. 12, 2026 at 9:35 a.m.; decision date not posted

items.title: PSC Districts 3 and 5 elections (Nov. 3, 2026) and control of the commission
items.status: Voted on Nov. 3, 2026; the page shows the live count and any race call; state certification is due by Nov. 20, 2026

In District 5, Republican Tricia Pridemore did not seek reelection (she ran for the U.S. House); Democrat Shelia Edwards, who won the May 19 Democratic primary, faced Republican Josh Tolbert, who won the June 16 Republican runoff over Bobby Mehan. The PSC website lists the current commission as Chairman Jason Shaw, Vice Chairman Lauren 'Bubba' McDonald, Peter Hubbard, Dr. Alicia M. Johnson and Stan Wise (District 5). Democrats won both PSC seats on the 2025 ballot (Hubbard and Alicia Johnson), their first statewide constitutional office wins since 2006, turning a 5-0 Republican commission into a 3-2 Republican majority; wins by both Hubbard and Edwards would give Democrats a 3-2 majority. Hubbard's campaign tied winning control of the commission to lowering power bills.

items.title: Transfer of the Atlanta City Detention Center (ACDC) to Fulton County
items.status: Framework presented at a Sept. 25, 2026 city-county work session; any transition is contingent on required legislative approvals; purchase discussions ongoing
items.summary: The City of Atlanta and Fulton County described a proposed framework under which Fulton County would acquire the Atlanta City Detention Center. The city would keep one floor and other administrative space to oversee its municipal detainees, and the Municipal Court, Solicitor's Office and Public Defender's Office would keep operating there. The Center for Diversion and Services, which has diverted more than 2,600 people from jail this year (about 60% through the Atlanta Police Department), would continue; the city pays half its operating costs and funded its renovations. The city is preparing placement in other city jobs, help finding outside work and possible retirement options for Department of Corrections employees, and the Fulton County Sheriff's Office said it welcomes city employees who want to continue law enforcement careers. No purchase price or timeline has been released.

items.summary: Savannah is drafting a zoning amendment that would define data centers as a land use for the first time and set development standards. Comments are taken at savannahga.gov/datacenters.

items.title: Lets property owners seek compensation from cities and counties that don't enforce camping, panhandling or sanctuary-policy bans
items.status: Signed by Gov. Kemp May 12, 2026 (Act 713); effective July 1, 2026
items.summary: Creates a claims process for real property owners against a city or county with a 'policy, pattern, or practice' of not enforcing state law on public camping and outdoor sleeping, loitering, panhandling, shoplifting or public drug use, or the state ban on immigration sanctuary policies. An owner first files a claim for documented expenses or lost fair market value; if the local government rejects it or does not act within 30 days, the owner may sue in superior court. It also lets people ask a court to order a local government to follow the ban on sanctuary policies. Final passage came in the session's last hours: House 93-76 on April 2, 2026, and Senate 34-19 (LegiScan records the roll call on April 3).
items.why: Supporters, including sponsor Rep. Houston Gaines, Sen. Clint Dixon and the Goldwater Institute (which backed a similar Arizona law), call it accountability for local governments; opponents, including the National Homelessness Law Center, the Georgia Latino Alliance for Human Rights, Sen. Josh McLaurin (D-Sandy Springs) and a City of Atlanta staff member, said it punishes homelessness and would burden the courts. Claims have been possible since July 1, 2026; no court rulings under the law were found in sources reviewed.
items.sponsors: Rep. Houston Gaines (R-Athens); carried in the Senate by Sen. Clint Dixon (R-Gwinnett)

items.title: Tougher lawsuits against local gun rules that go beyond state law, aimed at Savannah's gun-in-car ordinance (vetoed)
items.status: Passed by the General Assembly; vetoed by Gov. Kemp May 12, 2026 (Veto V10). Sources differ on the date of final passage: LegiScan records Senate agreement to the House version (32-21) on Jan. 13, 2026, while NRA-ILA described final passage at sine die.
items.summary: As rewritten by the House, SB 204 would have strengthened Georgia's firearm preemption law by expanding the lawsuits gun owners can bring against cities and counties that regulate guns beyond state and federal law: it increased the statutory damages available and removed the requirement that suits be brought against the county or city that enacted the rule, which Gov. Kemp said would open law enforcement officers to suits in their personal capacity. It targeted ordinances like Savannah's, which carries a fine of up to $1,000 and up to 30 days in jail for leaving a gun in an unlocked vehicle. The House passed it 99-74 on April 4, 2025, and the Senate agreed 32-21 on Jan. 13, 2026. Heather Hallett of Georgia Majority for Gun Safety celebrated the veto as a victory; Savannah Mayor Van Johnson defended the city's ordinance, crediting it with cutting reported gun thefts in Savannah by half from 2024 to 2025.
items.why: Kemp wrote that it 'would open the door to lawsuits against law enforcement officers, including in their personal capacity' and that 'such penalties should be targeted towards the leaders who enact such ordinances.' House carrier Rep. Alan Powell said the measure could return next year, and the Georgia Recorder reported Attorney General Chris Carr filed a brief supporting a lawsuit against Savannah's ordinance. A separate 2026 bill to remove suppressors from the state's dangerous-weapons list (SB 499) fell short at sine die.
items.sponsors: Former Sen. Colton Moore (R-Trenton), author; carried in the House by Rep. Alan Powell (R-Hartwell)

items.title: Medical cannabis expansion: ends the 5% THC cap, allows vaping, adds qualifying conditions (Putting Georgia's Patients First Act)
items.status: Signed by Gov. Kemp May 12, 2026, with a signing statement; took effect July 1, 2026
items.summary: Renames low-THC oil as medical cannabis and replaces the 5% THC cap with milligram limits (the Georgia House release cites a 1,200-milligram per-package limit; FOX 5 reports patients may possess up to 12,000 milligrams). Registered patients over 21 may vaporize products, while smoking and public use remain banned. It adds qualifying conditions including lupus, autism, Stage III HIV, severe Alzheimer's disease and inflammatory bowel disease, issues registration cards valid for five years, and gives the Georgia Access to Medical Cannabis Commission a seed-to-sale tracking system and fines of up to $25,000 for a licensee's first violation.

items.title: Georgia Pathways (Medicaid with work requirements) extended through Dec. 31, 2026
items.status: Federal approval announced Sept. 25, 2025; the extension runs Oct. 1, 2025 through Dec. 31, 2026
items.summary: The federal Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services approved a temporary extension of Georgia Pathways to Coverage, which offers Medicaid to low-income adults who report qualifying activities such as work, job training, education or volunteering. The extension counts parenting a Medicaid-enrolled child under 6 as a qualifying activity, requires members to report qualifying activities and hours only at application and annual renewal, and starts coverage on the first day of the month in which an application is received. items.title: Atlanta's $60 million homelessness plan and the pre-World Cup housing push
items.status: Plan announced Sept. 3, 2024 (Council approval not confirmed in sources opened); as of July 23, 2026, a $45 million gap remained in the $235 million 'Atlanta Rising' framework
items.summary: Mayor Andre Dickens and the City Council proposed $60 million for homelessness, which the city called the largest such investment in its history: a $50 million Homeless Opportunity Bond plus $10 million from the Affordable Housing Trust Fund over six years, for up to 700 units, including 500 quick-delivery modular units on city land through the Rapid Housing Initiative (targeted by the end of 2025) and up to 200 permanent supportive housing units. Partners for HOME said in July 2026, after the FIFA World Cup, that its outreach teams had led to 540 people moving into permanent housing over the previous 18 months. As of July 2026 its 'Atlanta Rising' plan to house 4,000 people over four years had a $45 million gap in a $235 million framework, and the latest point-in-time count showed homelessness up 6% to about 3,060 people.
items.why: Partners for HOME CEO Cathryn Vassell said city leaders rejected punitive measures such as busing and arrests, and that the group must find a sustainable source of revenue to close the gap; the state's HB 295 now also lets property owners file claims against cities that don't enforce camping bans.
items.sponsors: Mayor Andre Dickens; Atlanta City Council; Partners for HOME (CEO Cathryn Vassell)
